name: Locked In: The Steel Contract That Destroys Margin
deck: When 85% of your steel sales are locked into annual contracts, a commodity price drop that lasts three months can wreck a year of earnings.
core_bet: Industrial steel producers face a timing mismatch between the raw materials they buy and the prices they lock in with customers. Fixed-price contracts mean steelmakers absorb commodity volatility on the input side while their selling prices remain frozen. When scrap and iron ore prices fall, mills bleed margin for a full contract cycle. When prices spike, they miss the upside until renegotiation. This contract lag can turn a company with solid volumes and high utilization into a net-loss business.

mechanism: Fixed-price contracts are a feature of industrial relationships, not a bug. Automakers and construction firms want price certainty for their own planning and margin protection. Steel mills agree to lock in prices for 12 months (or longer) in exchange for volume commitments and relationship stability. This works fine when commodity costs are stable. It breaks catastrophically when they are not.

The mechanism is asymmetric exposure. A steelmaker locks in a selling price for the calendar year, say $1,200 per ton for hot-rolled coil. Its scrap costs—the primary input for electric-arc-furnace mills—are indexed to spot markets and move weekly. If scrap falls from $450/ton to $350/ton, the mill still receives $1,200 but now pays $100 less per ton in raw material. That sounds like a win. But if scrap started at $400/ton, the mill priced the contract assuming a $800 spread. The collapse in scrap has destroyed the margin calculation, and the mill cannot raise customer prices until next year's renegotiation or contract renewal.

Cleveland-Cliffs in 2025 experienced this in reverse. Fixed annual contracts were priced when automotive demand and steel markets looked stronger than they turned out to be. The company's management disclosed that flat-rolled volumes were sold at contract prices that lagged behind the reality of declining end-market demand and input cost pressure. Even worse, the company had a slab contract that management explicitly called 'value-destructive' in its final year. That means CMC was shipping material at prices so low that every ton sold reduced quarterly earnings. The company could not exit the contract without breaching customer agreements. It had to run the loss until expiration.

The timing lag creates a cash-consumption trap. Steel mills with fixed-price contracts become involuntary hedges on commodity volatility, absorbing losses during downturns and missing upside during rallies. Cleveland-Cliffs reported $37 million adjusted EBITDA for full-year 2025 despite managing 4+ million tons of shipments per quarter and deploying substantial manufacturing assets. The company was fundamentally solvent and well-run, but contract structure imprisoned its earnings. Commercial Metals saw the inverse in 2026: it achieved $111/ton margin improvement year-over-year in Q3, but that was possible only because customer prices finally rose to catch up to input costs that had already climbed in the prior year's contracts.
why_now: In 2024-2025, steel and scrap prices entered a prolonged decline after years of post-pandemic inflation. Mills had locked in customer contracts at prices set in 2023-2024 when inputs cost far more. The gap between locked selling prices and falling commodity costs widened for 9-12 months before the next renegotiation window. Cleveland-Cliffs' explicit disclosure of a 'value-destructive' slab contract signals that some mills had entered customer agreements at such low margins that each additional ton shipped was economically destructive. This happened not because of incompetence, but because the forecasting and contract-pricing process is backward-looking by design. Contracts signed in October reflect expectations set in August or September. If conditions reverse in November, mills are locked in until October the following year. The 2025-2026 cycle is particularly acute because industrial demand (especially automotive) remained weak while raw material costs fell sharply, leaving the gap between locked-in selling prices and lower input costs unfilled for extended periods.
who_pays: Workers and equipment utilization suffer first. When margins collapse due to contract lag, mills do not shut immediately. They keep running because fixed costs are so high that any positive contribution margin justifies operation. That means employment often holds steady even as profits vanish. Bondholders and shareholders absorb losses. Cleveland-Cliffs reported $1.4B net loss in 2025, a hit to equity value and credit ratings. Management responds by cutting capex (Cleveland-Cliffs guided for reduced capex and extended debt maturities), deferring maintenance, and negotiating contract amendments with customers. Customers themselves face pressure only after renegotiation windows. Automakers and construction firms benefit from the lag in their favor when prices fall (they lock in lower contracts), but they lose when prices rise and mills demand higher prices at renewal.
who_profits: Spot-market scrap recyclers and suppliers who can pivot quickly benefit when input costs fall faster than mill selling prices do. They capture the tail end of pricing before mill customers pass through increases in their own products. Steelmakers with higher proportions of spot or variable-index pricing (relative to fixed contracts) win during volatile periods. Nucor's disclosure that 85% of sheet sales are contract-based means 15% trade at spot prices, creating a hedge and earnings buffer during lag periods. Integrated miners like Cleveland-Cliffs that own both raw materials and milling can sometimes offset losses by running raw-material segments at lower losses. But the dominant beneficiary is simply time: mills benefit once contracts renew and prices reset. Commercial Metals saw $111/ton margin expansion in Q3 2026 because contracts signed a year earlier finally reflected the lower input costs that had prevailed continuously since the prior year's signing date.
tension: The contract structure that gives customers certainty and mills volume commitments is the same structure that traps mills in losses during downturns. Reducing fixed-price exposure would calm volatility for mills but would risk losing customer relationships and market share to competitors who offer price certainty. Mills cannot solve the problem unilaterally; they need customer agreement. During commodity downturns, customers have leverage and refuse renegotiation. During upswings, margins are healthy enough that mills do not push for change. The tension is structural: the incentive to fix the system exists only when margins are already acceptable, which is precisely when customers have no reason to renegotiate.
surprising_part: The most counterintuitive finding is that contract lag can produce massive accounting losses during periods of volume strength. Cleveland-Cliffs shipped 4+ million tons per quarter in 2025-2026, maintained substantial manufacturing capacity, employed 25,000 workers, and achieved positive operating cash flow. Yet it reported a $1.4B net loss in 2025 and negative adjusted EBITDA in Q4 2025. This is not a demand collapse or asset impairment story. This is a pure contract-pricing gap. A fully solvent, operational company can be pinned into net-loss territory by the simple fact that its customer agreements are priced in the past while its commodity costs are priced in the present. The company does not fail; it just bleeds cash to the balance sheet, deferring recovery until the next contract cycle begins.
one_sentence: Fixed-price steel contracts turn mills into involuntary absorbers of commodity volatility, forcing them to either run losses for a full 12-month cycle or breach customer agreements.
societal_stake: Steel and fabricated metals flow into every piece of infrastructure: bridges, buildings, vehicles, power systems, and data centers. When mills are trapped in losses due to contract lag, they defer maintenance, cut capex, and reduce hiring. This delays capacity expansion for the next infrastructure cycle and can create bottlenecks when demand returns. The 2025-2026 cycle shows that even in a period of stated industrial policy support and infrastructure spending, the commodity-contract mismatch can throttle material supply. Customers (automotive, construction) feel this as longer lead times and pricing uncertainty once renegotiations begin. The broader economy feels it as delayed factory expansions and reduced willingness to invest in new mill capacity.
